item.title: You Can Check Arkansas Off The List
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: After spending the last month in Memphis, it apparently became time for a brief weekend saunter to a campground outside of town for a lil’ break and to make sure Bessie still works, so off I went the nearest State Park an hour away in Arkansas. The fridge broke, but other than that the old [...]
item.content:encoded:
After spending the last month in Memphis, it apparently became time for a brief weekend saunter to a campground outside of town for a lil’ break and to make sure Bessie still works, so off I went the nearest State Park an hour away in Arkansas.  The fridge broke, but other than that the old girl is still holding up fine…

My fire poker, which is actually the size of my pinky

With Forrest City being the town closest to the park (and possessing a Walmart for supplies…hell, it’s Arkansas, Walmart is a landmark), the name immediately conjured up images of oak trees and owls nestled around pristine lakes and rivers.  While this may indeed by the case, it’s a funny thing how one extra R in Forrest changes the meaning greatly.  Yes, that would be Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Civil War general and founding member of the KKK, there’s a giant statue of him in Nashville too, but you know, this is the South, so they’re clearly only revering his Civil War tactical mastery and nothing else and if you say any different you better shut your mouth.  I’m not sure if the fact there’s a majority black population is Forrest City is funny, ironic or something I shouldn’t be talking about.

Back at the zoo in Memphis

I had seen Arkansas more than once as I trudged up the Mississippi Delta in November, but honestly had no intention of ever crossing the river.  I won’t be visiting any major cities or interacting with many locals in the forest, so I’ll have to reserve judgement, but…it seems nice?  Bill Clinton is from here, he’s a man.  And as a random aside, over the last four weeks I have met two different people who mentioned they had visited all 50 states.  Why anyone would do that is beyond me (apologies to South Dakota and Nebraska) and considering I’ve only been to 13 states in the last year and a half, I don’t want to be driving around until 2017 just to say I saw Mt. Rushmore.  Or do I…?

Regardless, to kill time at the campground I busted out the old extension tubes for the camera lens and took a few macro shots, and tagged on some from the Memphis zoo to make the gallery.

item.title: Mardi Gras 2012
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Well, that weekend was bat shit insane. I’m also astonished I made it out relatively unscathed. It’s also one of the few times you’ll ever hear me say this about anything…believe the hype. Without going way overboard on tales of bohemian fascination, the immense character of the city, that everyone will have a “New Orleans [...]
item.content:encoded:
Well, that weekend was bat shit insane.  I’m also astonished I made it out relatively unscathed.  It’s also one of the few times you’ll ever hear me say this about anything…believe the hype.

Without going way overboard on tales of bohemian fascination, the immense character of the city, that everyone will have a “New Orleans moment” and it’s way safer than advertized plus you can drink on the street, well, all those things are true.  And beads and parade floats and costumes and brass bands and genuine people everywhere, both locals and tourists.

Hundreds of floats like this all weekend

After being somewhat terrified at the Muses parade Thursday realizing it was a whole weekend of that, except many thousands more people, I got in the swing quick.  Thursday was also the only day I bothered to venture out with my actual camera, so that gallery is here (not that pictures do it any justice).

On Friday after proclaiming the day before I wasn’t really big into parades, there I was back again near the start of the route in the garden district jumping up and down like a school girl waving to people on the floats for throws (my total count for the weekend was around 25 strings of beads, 2 footballs, 1 frisbee and 1 plastic cup, and I wasn’t trying).  Wandering up Magazine, or maybe Tchoupitoulas, I stopped to chat with a bunch of kids my age who lived in a house right on the parade route.  Within minutes the high fives, dance moves, and handle of Jack Daniels being passed around were all flowing freely.  I was aided in making fast friends because one of the residents had lived in Saskatchewan at some point, so got Canadian props.  Eventually I sheepishly asked to use his bathroom as those are coveted like nothing else on the parade route, then I found I never really left the house once the full drum kit and guitars came out for jamming and the bong started going around, then I have no idea what happened because I forgot to eat dinner, but I made it back to Bessie alright although I must have fallen down a few times.

Sexy shiny dancers

Saturday poured rain, I won’t bore you with the details of that or Sunday, but Monday, a.k.a. Lundi Gras is the big party day.  The cops even show up on Bourbon Street at midnight to clear everybody out, I only made it over there once and it’s not my crowd, there’s so many better places and cheaper bars with more character.  Like for example, Parasol’s, rumoured to be where the Po’Boy was first invented and open since the 1950’s.  It was there dealing with the one and a half hour wait for two sandwiches with a friend I’d made earlier in the week that we met Frank and Leroy…

Sitting on a sunny stoop across the street as every table was full, a man in his 50s with wild wavy hair and a sequined Mardi Gras visor came over in his wheelchair and informed us he called this “the office” because he’d always sit there and drink with his acquaintances, which was every single person who walked by.  Having been diagnosed with MS a few years earlier definitely didn’t slow Frank down, in fact it probably sped him up thanks to her service dog Leroy, a beautiful and friendly red lab.  Within minutes, Frank asked if we wanted to see him go, so he went out in the street, screamed “GO!!” and off Leroy went.  They have apparently been clocked at 19 mph as you can learn from this local news segment about the two of them.

That about sums it up

After hearing of Frank’s plan to run for congress, how he partied with Cyndi Lauper in the 80’s, that he was going on tour with his one man guitar set when his record came out in a month and how he wanted me to get a ramp into Bessie so I could be his tour bus, well, you get the picture.  Then the reporter who did the story stopped by with the weather girl for a visit and a drink at “the office”.  Then…

OK, that was 3:30 PM and I stayed out until about 2, so you can guess for yourself plenty more happenned, but I’ll stop rambling.  I was originally going to say that everyone should do Mardi Gras at least once in their life (well, if they’re young, or young at heart and like to party) but I can tell you this, I’ll be going back for another.

item.title: Who’s Tom Petty?
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Yes, someone actually asked me that. We were talking about concerts we’d been to and I referenced him at the once-of Pemberton Festival in Canada, and just got a blank stare. I’m not sure if it’s worse or better that I followed up, eyebrow raised with “y’know…Last Dance With Mary Jane…Free Fallin’?” and got “oh [...]
item.content:encoded:
Yes, someone actually asked me that.  We were talking about concerts we’d been to and I referenced him at the once-of Pemberton Festival in Canada, and just got a blank stare.  I’m not sure if it’s worse or better that I followed up, eyebrow raised with “y’know…Last Dance With Mary Jane…Free Fallin’?” and got “oh yeah, sure I know those” without pressing to verify they weren’t just saying that to get the horrified look off my face.

Fine, I'll just go listen to Tom Petty by myself!

I believe it was Plato who famously complained about the youths these days, and having been proven wrong over thousands of years it’s something I make a conscious effort to try not to say or believe even if deep down I sympathize.  Being in the college town of Gainesville, home to the University of Florida (yes, Tim Tebow’s alma matter, we’ll skip that commentary here) I figured it only made sense to CouchSurf with some college kids, so I broke my rule of not seeking out people more than 5 years my junior.  Oh I don’t regret it, we went to an Oregon Trail themed party and a rager house party with 50 people at a three bedroom house mainly spilling out onto the street.  There was even a dude with a mullet and a shirt that read GAINESVILLE FUCKING FLORIDA!

However, because this is the American south, the term we use in Canada called “student ghetto” still applies, but in a literal sense.  A transient kid population just looking for a cheap place to live begets slum lords, rundown properties and depressed values, which in turn causes actual riff raff to move in.  I didn’t really think much of some of the neighbours coming over and crashing the party, other than laughing that kids had the audacity to complain when there was blaring music and 40 people blocking the street at two in the morning.  Soon enough someone had ordered a Jimmy John sandwich, the delivery boy propped his bike on the side of the house when he went in to deliver it, then found it gone when he came back outside.  Quickly borrowing someone else’s bike to search for his own, after some minutes he angrily sped back towards the full crowd, someone stepped in his way and he totally wiped in front of all the cool kids and threw his helmet against the wall screaming he would shit in their sandwich if they ever ordered one to that house again.

***

“What’s espresso?”

For some reason this question from the person in front of me in line brought a beaming grin to my face, unlike the Tom Petty inquiry.  It was in response to the scripted sales pitch at McDonald’s for their new McCafe deal, and if it wasn’t for the piece of paper to answer, I’m pretty sure the cashier didn’t know either.  By this point in time I was in the absolute middle of nowhere in the Florida panhandle, returning from another adventure of camping in the middle of nowhere (best spot ever FYI, check the gallery).  It was the only McDonald’s for 50 miles in any direction, there probably wasn’t a Starbucks, or for that matter an espresso maker for at least 100, and I’m not sure why, but I like that, even though I like espresso, and Starbucks.

The Gulf

What I didn’t like was hearing the 6 year old kid in the booth next to me make reference to “the 51 states” and not be corrected by her mother.  I mean, maybe Puerto Rico counts because this is Florida, but these were white country folks in the panhandle.  Somehow miraculously diffusing the reaction growing in my mind was the fact I was drawn into it as the mother turned to me and asked while pointing to the parking lot “what state does that license plate say, New York?”  It was very far away, but I have fighter pilot vision and have been able to beat anyone reading the letters at a distance since I was a child, so after a brief squint I informed her “no ma’am, Michigan”.  Thank God Bessie was out of view so we didn’t have to get into which state Alberta was.

item.title: Beware the Rainbows: An Ode to the Turkey Vulture
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: The more life, the more death, the more vultures. Effortless in the gentlest of wind, feathered wings spread wide, always exactly an hour before sundown they begin to soar by the dozens, one must always be the first to take flight, the rest following within seconds. Their penchant for carrion unseen belies the lushness of [...]
item.content:encoded:
The more life, the more death, the more vultures.  Effortless in the gentlest of wind, feathered wings spread wide, always exactly an hour before sundown they begin to soar by the dozens, one must always be the first to take flight, the rest following within seconds.  Their penchant for carrion unseen belies the lushness of the Florida forest.  Discordant with most wildernesses across the continent, the escaped housecat in feral form is the dominant species, but it shrinks from view in the light.  The alligator does so accidentally as a result of its nature; its thrashing prey’s death throes at sundown far too loud to have ever feigned camouflage.

Vultures are fucking hippies.  Everyone else does all the work, they spend all their time high as the goddam sky swooping in for a freebie whenever they can, and I love them for it.

Acton, Florida

But the tick…upon finding the first ever in my life latched to my thigh, I plucked it while musing “I have fabricated the evolution of man from antiquity to modernity solely within my own mind, the internal combustion engine facilitating my journey of thousands of miles, only to be the vehicle for the greatest distance you will ever travel, from shrubbery bush to squashed fingertip residue.  At least I have the capacity to pretend I have hopes and a will of my own, and to perhaps falsely ascribe the same virtues to the vulture.  But you tick, are an automaton, feeding without knowing.”

***

Having done “civilization” for far too long, I decided to return to my western US roots by boondocking in the middle of nowhere in Florida’s Ocala National Forest.  Problem is, being an hour from Orlando and the ocean in Daytona Beach, this isn’t the middle of nowhere like, oh, all of New Mexico.

Lake Eaton

My sanctioned $8 a night campground hosts at Lake Eaton told me of a couple free places to park in the middle of the forest, but warned me to watch out for “rainbows”.  I had already come across what that meant in Florida-speak researching the area online, so proddingly asked “you mean gypsies?”  To which I got the amazing response “no, worse…hippies.”  Fucking hippies!

Funny thing is, they use that term pretty loosely, it really just means vagabonds with unwashed hair, and there’s a huge difference.  When I heard tales of bonfires, yelling and drinking until 1 AM, that sounded like something to seek out, not avoid.  Yet when I drove 3 miles down the highway and saw at least a half dozen people with dreadlocks, a pitbull and their thumbs stuck out on the side of the road, I realized this unsanctioned campsite may very well have been the mistake the 60 year olds made it out to be.

Scowls.  Scowls that I knew of their perch in the bush where the ranger only stopped by once a week to boot them out.  A scowl like I got giving an extremely (and accidentally) quizzical look to the man who walked into Burger King a week ago in Daytona Beach demanding free food with the unspoken threat that he would either start screaming uncontrollably or shit in the middle of the floor.  Oh he got his food, the manager even knew his name, but I know now that he was a rainbow, not a hippie…a tick, not a vulture.

item.title: Space is the place
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Ah to be back in a Walmart parking lot in the middle of nowhere. Well, apologies to the residents of Deltona, Florida, but being exactly halfway between Orlando and Daytona Beach, this isn’t exactly a destination. I did appreciate the naming of the bar across the street as the Sports Den, before even entering there [...]
item.content:encoded:
Ah to be back in a Walmart parking lot in the middle of nowhere.  Well, apologies to the residents of Deltona, Florida, but being exactly halfway between Orlando and Daytona Beach, this isn’t exactly a destination.  I did appreciate the naming of the bar across the street as the Sports Den, before even entering there were no bones about the fact I would be surrounded by degenerate 60 year olds bitching about their ex-wives and saying all kinds of shit to the lovely and barely 21 barkeep Sammi knowing she had to put up with it to get her tips.

Open the pod bay doors

FYI, I’ve been doing a belated Christmas with my parents the last 8 days after refusing to return home for the holidays.  It was alright then, but currently is -30 in Calgary, so I stand by my decision to not take the chance.  I’ll take the Kennedy Space Center, Sea World and fresh shrimp over ski hills, overpriced drinks and everyone pretending we don’t live in Siberia any day of the week.

Just to expand on a point I made in my last post (yeah, I know they’re getting less frequent, eat me), I do laugh at the international perception of Americans as jackasses the deeper I get into tourist locations.  I forget how much closer Disney World is than Disney Land to Europe, so the concentration of our friends from across the pond is dramatically higher in Florida than California.  And when you’re standing in a grocery store with a 6 deep line and a 13 year old kid with a thick Italian accent walks right up to the front when the cashier is ringing someone else through and yells “hey, hey, HEY!  How much this costs?!?!” it all becomes clear.  Yes, Americans are loud and obnoxious, and to some degree entitled.  But at that exact moment it made me realize that the type of American that is able to be a globetrotter (only 20% have passports) must have money, probably thinks they’re better than everyone and is an asshole, probably fitting the exact same demographic of Europeans coming here.

R.I.P. Yuri

Ummm, I have no point whatsoever here.  But I took a bunch of fun pictures of Cocoa Beach and Orlando, check them out in the gallery.

item.title: North America is my bitch
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: The Atlantic. Wait, the Atlantic Ocean? The Atlantic anticlimax? As quickly as the Georgia pines of last week turned to palm trees, so too did the New Mexico desert of 8 months ago give way to sandy Florida beaches and me staring towards Spain. So FYI, it’s not that difficult to drive all the way [...]
item.content:encoded:
The Atlantic.  Wait, the Atlantic Ocean?  The Atlantic anticlimax?  As quickly as the Georgia pines of last week turned to palm trees, so too did the New Mexico desert of 8 months ago give way to sandy Florida beaches and me staring towards Spain.

Now this is happenning, the Atlantic

So FYI, it’s not that difficult to drive all the way from coast to coast in America, even if it takes you 12 months.  And you’ll see a lot, and eat and drink just as much.  You might also find that camping under the stars in the middle of nowhere is just as rewarding as plopping down on a bar stool next to one of the 300 million people that live here.  They’re all very different depending on where you go, but football and beer some to be pretty common threads.

I lost track of where I was going anymore sometime around the middle of Texas.  Now I’m just a guy in a van.  A friend wondered this before I even began my journey, when I would become “guy in van”, and that happened at the exact same time in middle Texas.  In the beginning it was like “wheee, look at me go!”, but then it gave way to “where am I going?”  But the real distinguishing mark is I don’t remember what it was like to think this whole idea was new and fresh and explain it to people like some revelation, because it’s not, it just is.  Not that I wouldn’t highly recommend it, and Bessie will be for sale in maybe 2 years when I get sick of this, but for now the south is pretty fantastic.  I also highly recommend quitting your job and telling anyone who will listen to play a game of hide and go fuck themselves.

Ocean still got forests

It’s become painfully obvious that anyone who doesn’t stop and say hello crossing paths with you on a nature trail or a not overly crowded city street is most likely from Europe, and the fact they generally start speaking French, German or Italian immediately thereafter is telling.  But even if they spoke fluent English, they wouldn’t stop to say hello, and I don’t know why.  You’d think I would have some insight, having never done it myself back in Canada, but it’s something American I can’t explain, same as how I picked up saying “riiiiight” every time I agree with someone.

The Florida coast is somewhat similar to the California coast, but with less money, which equates to more charm if you aren’t rolling around with a few thousand in your pocket.  Jacksonville Beach, St. Augustine, sure there’s plenty of nice stuff, but you don’t have to be a millionaire to live there, and a bar with a $2 pint or a pornography super-warehouse are never too far.  Even Jekyll Island in Georgia where I took all these shots, I didn’t even clue in as to why there were 4 golf courses on a tiny island with a campground, then getting there to find a castle, marina and “Millionaire’s row”, well I was still able to camp in a lovely spot of $20 a night, and I’ll gladly spend that all the way down to the everglades.

item.title: I’m Officially A Snowbird
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I’m pretty sure the icing on the cake was me spending New Years Eve at a potluck full of 65 year olds at the group shelter at the Little Ocmulgee campground in the middle of nowhere in Georgia. Either that, or me kicking everyone’s ass at dominos until they got too tired and went to [...]
item.content:encoded:
I’m pretty sure the icing on the cake was me spending New Years Eve at a potluck full of 65 year olds at the group shelter at the Little Ocmulgee campground in the middle of nowhere in Georgia.  Either that, or me kicking everyone’s ass at dominos until they got too tired and went to bed at 10 PM.  Or maybe the $15 round of golf I played with three of them the next day.

New Years Resolution: Drink more of this!

My one saving grace was that not surprisingly, everyone was Canadian.  They all get too sick of the cold and make the 15 hour drive from Ontario to Georgia to spend the winter as campground hosts, it’s surprisingly not as far as you’d think, unless you move at my pace.  And as a note to future retired self, the campground (or golf course) host/volunteer gig is a pretty good one.  Stay as long as you want for free, golf for free every day all in turn for maybe 2 to 3 hours of light chores each day, such as spending 30 minutes touring young Canadian fellows like myself around in a golf cart when they arrive then maybe grabbing them a pile of wood or replacing a light bulb in the bathroom.

Dude was a slick dresser

The whole experience was almost frighteningly Canadian, actually.  Where at the Sardis Lake campground in Mississippi on Thanksgiving I tried talking to the locals next to me and they were so terrified of my long hair they didn’t even respond, at Little Ocmulgee I’d chatted about Belleville Ontario, the exchange rate and how cheap beer was down here for 15 minutes before I’d even selected a campsite.

To recap since Nashville, which was only a week ago, I’ve gone through Lynchburg Tennessee and the Jack Daniels Distillery, which wasn’t worth writing about because arriving at 2:30 got me a chance to take the tour at 4, although that was the last time I took the camera out so those are all the attached shots.  Then on to Chattanooga, where I still don’t understand the significance of the Choo Choo, but it’s a very upscale chic town with a great microbrewery called the Terminal Brewhouse.  Atlanta is too sprawling, horrifyingly large and easy to get in the wrong part of town that I just skipped through it, and then on to Macon, where the whole place is the wrong part of town, although I was able to work a karaoke crowd with another rousing rendition of Desperado, which I’ve determined is a hit down here because it’s sort of, kind of a country song.

Stay mellow in 2012, y'all

So here I am in Brunswick, Georgia, 10 minutes away from the Atlantic Ocean wanting to save it until tomorrow so I can fully savour the triumph of making it all the way across the continent.  I’m not planning on zig-zagging all the way back, and have nothing planned beyond a little Florida time next week, but I’m still pretty sure 2012 will have some big things in store for the Blimpster as I have no intention of stopping any time soon.

item.title: A lil’ bit Country
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: “I love your hat, where’d you get it?” the waitress asked of the pink-sequined Santa hat I was wearing as we ate sushi. “I found it on the floor last night at an ugly sweater party at Blue Bar. Frosty the snow man was DJing.” I still think it has some potential to become a [...]
item.content:encoded:
“I love your hat, where’d you get it?” the waitress asked of the pink-sequined Santa hat I was wearing as we ate sushi.

The hat repetoir grows

“I found it on the floor last night at an ugly sweater party at Blue Bar.  Frosty the snow man was DJing.”  I still think it has some potential to become a seasonal pimp hat (it’s more fuchsia than pink), but her quizzical eye wrinkle at the floor bit made me realize the line needs some refining.  Good thing I didn’t tell her about the forgotten soldier beer I randomly picked off the bar and drank later in the night, it was still three quarters full and coldish, so basically the deal of the night.

Rewinding, I have been in Nashville for over a week now, sorry I skipped over my post on Memphis.  I think that’s because the most poignant observations I had were the “6 block rule” that no matter how safe you are, walk six blocks and you aren’t, that Terrence Howard’s accent in Hustle and Flow was way off but Ludacris had it bang on and that 11 AM is a really busy time at the convenience store because there will be 4 people ahead of you buying 40s.  Crazy good weed though, nothing like rolling around with my 6’8” buddy Tre at 2 AM on a Friday rockin some “strawberry cough” reminiscing about his days playing college ball in Arkansas.

OK, the DJ wasn't country

Up here in Music City, I’ve been staying with one of the most talented keyboardists you’ve ever met, so far hitting up a few recording studios, the Hammond repair shop, meeting a wide variety of musicians and song-writers, watching my Calgary Flames lose because they actually have a hockey team here, and just being generally busy.  ‘tis the season I suppose.

I kinda feel bad having a whole gallery of phone camera shots, but I’ve been coming across all kinds of stuff.  Apparently the thing to do is build a recording studio in your own basement so you don’t have to book time and can overdub tracks in your underwear and still get paid, but watching someone putting 2-inch stops under the new door frame in their severely curved/sunken 130 year old home makes me laugh at a new adage I have heard about recording studios.  They’re like a boat, a lot more fun when you’ve got a buddy who owns one.

item.title: The Delta Diaries: The Sound and the Fury
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: OK, so Oxford isn’t actually in the Delta as evidenced by the fact there are hills, but it’s close enough, and I absolutely adore alliteration. Here’s the gallery. Home to all things William Faulkner and the legendary university Ole’ Miss, Oxford sticks out like a sore thumb versus the rest of northern Mississippi. A rich, [...]
item.content:encoded:
OK, so Oxford isn’t actually in the Delta as evidenced by the fact there are hills, but it’s close enough, and I absolutely adore alliteration.  Here’s the gallery.

One bourbon, one scotch, one Faulkner

Home to all things William Faulkner and the legendary university Ole’ Miss, Oxford sticks out like a sore thumb versus the rest of northern Mississippi.  A rich, white, antebellum thumb steeped in tradition to the point many would tell you it’s the absolute epicentre of “the South”, and I would have a tough time arguing against that.  Students attend their football games in khaki suits and summer dresses and the only time you can buy alcohol on a Sunday is if Ole’ Miss had a home game the day before, which unfortunately wasn’t the case the Sunday I rolled in.

It also happens to be the school James Meredith enrolled at in 1962, forcing Kennedy to send in the National Guard to stop the riots with him being their first black student.  He was subsequently shot on a march from Memphis to Jackson in 1966, but survived, although I’m told no one showed up to see him speak on the 40th anniversary of his enrolment, well, no one who was white.  Tough life being a hero.

Gorgeous town, tons of history

Another great Ole’ Miss story was them deciding to retire their mascot Colonel Rebel in 2003 because it was deemed to be racist due to his costume as a plantation owner.  However, when your team name is the Rebels, there’s a memorial to all who died fighting the Union in the center of campus and your state flag still has the Confederate flag on it, who’s kidding who and what does it matter?  Apparently all merchandize bearing the Colonel’s likeness stopped being sold by the school, but some local business/historical folks started the Colonel Reb Foundation, secured rights to his likeness and are now able to profit off him instead.

There was a long, drawn-out fight/vote/what-have-you to try and name a replacement and they somehow arrived at the Rebel Black Bear, even though there isn’t a sizeable population of black bears in this region of Mississippi and he has yet to make an appearance at a game.  At a local bar named Roosters ($2 pitchers on Monday, 3 stories, 3 bars in one…ugh it still hurts) they sell t-shirts with the Colonel flipping the bird and the caption “Bear This!” that sell by the thousands.  So like I said originally, what was the point?  The Washington Redskins is still a million times worse when you think about it.

Not good RV weather

My month in Mississippi is now drawing to a close as I head towards Memphis, but I must say the Delta has without a doubt been the most memorable stop of my entire journey.  Not that I would recommend it for everyone, but I have learned an incredible amount about society past and present, which I think was part of my adventure’s goal, along with the striking scenery this area has.  Unfortunately even in the South they get a little something called winter, which I was not expecting, so after Nashville I’m pretty sure I’ll be making a bee line for Florida.

item.title: The Delta Diaries: Travelling Riverside Blues
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Friar’s point, Vicksburg, Rosedale, at least I’ve been to all the places Robert Johnson mentions in the song. Nobody’s squeezed my lemon ‘til the juice runs down my leg yet…not that I have any clue what that’s supposed to mean… Travelling back in time to the pilgrimage to his gravesite a few weeks ago (at [...]
item.content:encoded:
Friar’s point, Vicksburg, Rosedale, at least I’ve been to all the places Robert Johnson mentions in the song.  Nobody’s squeezed my lemon ‘til the juice runs down my leg yet…not that I have any clue what that’s supposed to mean…

R.I.P. King of the Delta Blues

Travelling back in time to the pilgrimage to his gravesite a few weeks ago (at least I think, time and space get thicker and muddled in the Delta) it was both a letdown and better than I hoped, as I’ve found with anywhere I have expectations about.  The number one problem was the dispute about where he was actually buried, there are three places in the vicinity of Greenwood Mississippi at one point laying claim, all still bearing grave markers.  Same goes for which jook joint he got poisoned at, or which plantation he crawled off to die at.  Even though the Little Zion M.B. Church I visited is the most believed burial ground, the marker there was placed in 2000 and is certainly not over top of Mr. Johnson’s body.

This is a shame because I had hoped to snag a blade of grass with some of his carbon atoms to put in a little pouch as part of my mojo hand, but I think I’m resigned to having my mojo hand just be in my head cuz I ain’t superstitious.  What’s also too bad is the marker was placed there by a fellow named Stephen LaVere, a local “historian” who used to run a Robert Johnson museum in town, which I read several reviews of it actually being a museum to himself.  Turns out he was just saving money to move to Hawaii and really had no allegiance to Greenwood at all, there’s still a note posted on the door offering to sell his Robert Johnson memorabilia collection as a whole or piecemeal, whichever nets the highest bid.  And honestly, who the hell puts their name on someone else’s grave marker?

I hung out here for at least an hour, amazingly tranquil

Spending this much time in the Delta is starting to give me my own travelling riverside blues, I’m a directionless fish out of water.  I don’t translate to people, nor them to me.  I tell my story, people think it’s ‘neat’, then within two minutes they are giving me their slant about all kinds of racist leanings they have, but telling me it’s “OK” because this is Mississippi, it’s honestly happened time and again.  There are still black and white high schools in most towns, I get that, it’s for complex historical reasons (called slavery, which you aren’t allowed to talk about), but once the conversation starts swaying to your grandmother not being able to get welfare because she’s white and we have a black president…wait, what?  You lost me.

It also definitely makes me realize that while I love Delta blues music, it doesn’t belong to me in any way shape or form, never will.  If this is what it’s like now, the 1930’s are surely unimaginable to my white Canadian brain.  I mean black people were still getting murdered in the 1960’s just for trying to register to vote.  And while I was originally asking a lot of people why there wasn’t more tourism in this area because it’s gorgeous, it’s still…I dunno…the Delta.  There’s something impenetrably thick about the place if you weren’t born and raised here, just walking down the street all kinds of folk (white folk, actually) stare at me up and down disdainfully for several seconds because I’m clearly not from around here.  Nobody wears sunglasses, nobody has long hair, that’s just the way it goes, and I’m more than willing to accept that acceptance doesn’t go both ways.

Uhhhh…happy Thanksgiving y’all!
